# File-type filtering in ripgrep

File-type filtering is what backs `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`,
`--type-clear` and `--type-list`. Almost all of it lives in the `ignore` crate,
in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` and `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. The
`core` crate only translates CLI flags into calls on the builder.

## How definitions are represented

The shipped definitions are a single constant in `default_types.rs`:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["ada"], &["*.adb", "*.ads"]),
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    ...
];
```

Each entry is a list of aliases paired with a list of globs. Aliases are not a
first-class concept downstream: `TypesBuilder::add_defaults` loops over the
names and registers each one separately, so `bat` and `batch` become two
independent definitions holding the same globs. The only invariant the crate
enforces is a unit test, `default_types_are_sorted`, which checks that the
*first* alias of each entry is strictly increasing. Duplicate globs across types
are fine and common (`cs` and `csharp` both carry `*.cs`).

A registered definition is a `FileTypeDef`, a `name: String` plus a
`globs: Vec<String>`. It exposes `name()` and `globs()` and nothing else. The
builder stores them in a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>`, so a name is
registered once and repeated `add` calls append globs to the existing entry.

`TypesBuilder` also keeps `selections: Vec<Selection<()>>`, an ordered log of
`Select(name)` / `Negate(name)` in the order the user asked for them. The
selection carries only a name at this stage; nothing is resolved against the
definition map until `build()`.

Two entry points create definitions. `add(name, glob)` takes them separately and
rejects `name == "all"` or any name containing a non-alphanumeric character
(`char::is_alphanumeric`, so Unicode letters and digits are accepted). `add_def`
parses the user-facing string form and delegates to `add`. It splits on `:` and
accepts exactly two shapes: `name:glob`, and `name:include:a,b,c`. The include
form checks that every referenced type already exists before touching anything,
then **copies** the referenced globs into the new definition. That copy is a
snapshot: a later `--type-add` to `cpp` or a `--type-clear cpp` does not
retroactively change a `src:include:cpp` defined earlier.

## How a matcher is built

`TypesBuilder::build()` produces a `Types`. It walks `self.selections` in order
and, for each one, resolves the name in the definition map. An unknown name is
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType`; that is what makes `--type-clear rust -trust`
fail rather than silently match nothing. Every glob of the resolved definition is
compiled with `GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)` and pushed into a
single `GlobSetBuilder`, and `glob_to_selection` records `(selection index, glob
index)` for each glob added, in lockstep with the set.

The result holds the compiled `GlobSet`, the resolved
`Vec<Selection<FileTypeDef>>`, `glob_to_selection`, and `has_selected`, a bool
set when at least one selection is non-negated. It also holds an
`Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` (`regex_automata::util::pool::Pool`) used as scratch
space for match indices, which is why `Types` can be cloned cheaply and shared
across the walker's threads.

## How matching works

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns `Match<Glob>`:

- Directories and an empty glob set return `Match::None` immediately. Type
  filtering never prunes traversal; it only rejects individual files.
- Only the **base name** is matched, via `pathutil::file_name`. Combined with
  `literal_separator(true)`, a type glob containing `/` can never match. If
  `file_name` returns `None` (paths ending in `.` or `..`), the result is
  `Ignore` when `has_selected`, else `None`.
- `set.matches_into` fills the pooled vec with matching glob indices in
  ascending order. `matches.last()` is therefore the highest-numbered matching
  glob, which by construction belongs to the **last selection on the command
  line**. That selection's `is_negated()` decides `Match::Ignore` versus
  `Match::Whitelist`. So `-tfoo -Trust` and `-Trust -tfoo` differ for a file
  matching both.
- With no glob match and `has_selected` true, the path is `Match::Ignore` with
  `Glob::unmatched()` (no `FileTypeDef` attached). This is the whitelist
  behaviour behind `-tall`.

`Ignore::matched` in `dir.rs` applies this after overrides and ignore files, so
`-g` and `.gitignore` outrank `-t`, matching the documented precedence.

## Notes for contributors

`select("all")` and `negate("all")` expand eagerly over the *current* keys of
the definition map, so `-tall --type-add 'foo:*.foo'` does not select `foo`
while the reverse order does. Ordinary selections resolve lazily at `build()`
and are order-insensitive against `--type-add`.

CLI wiring is `types()` in `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs`, which replays
`LowArgs::type_changes` (a `Vec<TypeChange>` in argv order) onto a builder
seeded with `add_defaults()`. `--type-list` is `main.rs::types`, printing
`Types::definitions()`, which sorts globs within a definition and definitions by
name, and exits 1 when the list is empty.

Adding a default type means one line in `DEFAULT_TYPES`, sorted, wrapped to 79
columns, with globs that only reference a file name. Behavioural changes want
coverage in the `matched!` table at the bottom of `types.rs` and, for flag-level
behaviour, in `tests/misc.rs` (`file_type_add`, `file_type_add_compose`,
`file_type_clear`). Note that `add` accepts an empty name (the
`chars().all(..)` check is vacuously true); only `add_def` rejects it, so any
new entry point should replicate that guard.
